# MassAssignmentException in Laravel

Encountering a `MassAssignmentException` during database seeding is one of the most common friction points for developers moving from raw SQL or early Laravel versions to modern Eloquent models. The error you are seeing, specifically regarding the `username` attribute, indicates that your model is actively preventing data from being written to the database under the circumstances you specified. This behavior is not a bug; it is a deliberate security feature designed to mitigate Mass Assignment Vulnerabilities, where an attacker might inject hidden fields into a form to escalate privileges or alter system state.

When you execute `php artisan db:seed --class="UsersTableSeeder"`, the `User::create()` method attempts to populate the database with the provided array. However, Eloquent checks this array against the model's fillable attributes before executing any SQL. If the `username` key exists in your input array but is not explicitly allowed by the model, Eloquent throws this exception to halt the operation immediately.

Your seed class attempts to create users with a `username`, `email`, and `password`. The error log points specifically to `username`. This means that somewhere in your `User` model definition, you have likely restricted which attributes can be mass-assigned. In older Laravel versions (prior to 5.6) or if using the default configuration without modification, all fillable fields were allowed by default, but modern installations often enforce strict rules out of the box.

To resolve this, you must inspect your `User` model file. You will likely find a `$fillable` property defined as an empty array:

```php
class User extends Model
{
    protected $fillable = [];
}
```

By setting `$fillable` to an empty array, the developer has opted into "strict" mass assignment mode. In this mode, only attributes explicitly listed in that array can be set via `create()` or `update()`. Since `username` is not in that list, Eloquent blocks the write operation and throws the exception you observed.

The solution is straightforward: add `username` to the `$fillable` property. You should also consider adding `email`, as it is standard practice to allow these core user attributes for seeding purposes. Update your model accordingly:

```php
protected $fillable = ['username', 'email', 'password'];
```

Once this change is applied, re-run your seeder command. The exception will vanish, and the users will be created successfully.

It is important to understand the trade-off here. While enabling these fields allows you to seed data easily, it opens a security gap for any other endpoint that accepts user input. If you have a registration form or an API controller that accepts a `username` field, you must ensure that the controller explicitly validates and sanitizes that input before passing it to the model. Never rely solely on `$fillable` to secure your application; always validate incoming requests.

If you prefer not to modify the model globallyâfor instance, if you are working with a shared library or a strict framework where models cannot be alteredâyou can disable mass assignment protection entirely by setting the `APP_PREVENT_STRICT_MODE` configuration option (in newer Laravel versions) or adding the `--no-strategy` flag depending on your specific setup. However, in most standard projects, modifying `$fillable` is the preferred approach because it maintains a clear separation between trusted seeding data and untrusted user input.

Remember that `password` is also sensitive. Even if you add it to `$fillable`, ensure you are hashing the password using `Hash::make()` before passing it to `User::create()`. Storing plain-text passwords like `'45678'` in your database is a critical security risk regardless of mass assignment settings.

For further guidance on securing your application and understanding attribute protection, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) offer deeper dives into Eloquent configuration and best practices for handling user data safely.
